title: Sound and lighting: common mistakes that ruin an event
excerpt: Equipment rarely fails in isolation. More often, the plan fails: soundcheck, microphones, electricity, lighting and music are not finalized on time. Here are the mistakes that cause embarrassing interruptions and how to prevent them without wasting money.

coverAlt: Event sound and lighting in Podgorica and Montenegro
segments: When the sound crackles or lighting ruins the atmosphere, guests do not remember the good food or decent programme. They remember interruptions, stress and the sense that something was wrong. Technical production is the foundation of the experience and must be planned as a system, not an afterthought settled the day before with a message to bring some speakers and lights.

In Podgorica and across Montenegro, most technical problems are not about poor equipment. They happen because nobody finalized the basics: who will speak, which microphone they will use, where speakers go, how much power is available, when soundcheck happens, who gives final approval and what to do if something fails.
Why technical mistakes hurt most

Technical production is the first thing an audience notices and the last thing it forgives. If a speaker cannot be heard, people disengage. If a microphone squeals, everyone loses focus. Poor lighting makes photos and videos look bad, leaving a lasting impression that the event was poorly run even if it was not. The objective is unobtrusive, calm and reliable technical execution.
Mistake 1: no soundcheck, or one squeezed in casually

Without a proper soundcheck, the first 20 minutes can bring squealing microphones, inaudible speeches, fluctuating music levels, an anxious host and technicians rushing around. Soundcheck needs a scheduled, protected slot - not whenever there is time.

A soundcheck is not just seeing whether the equipment works. Check how voices sound, whether volume is stable, whether people in the back can hear clearly without echo, how microphones behave when speakers turn their heads and whether music overpowers speech. Smaller venues in Podgorica may sound good at the front and poor at the back. Catch that before guests arrive.
Mistake 2: the wrong microphone type

Choose microphones for the situation, not merely for availability. Typical mistakes include using one handheld for everyone, badly placed clip-on microphones that rustle or passing a microphone around the audience so slowly that the programme stalls.

For speeches and panels, a clip-on or headset microphone plus a spare handheld often works well. For Q&A, a runner carrying a handheld microphone to the questioner preserves the pace. For the host, use a handheld with spare batteries, as they speak frequently and move around the stage.
The failure is not always that the microphone stops working; it is the time lost changing microphones, replacing batteries and getting people set up. Corporate audiences notice that immediately.
Mistake 3: underestimating power and cables

Household extension cords and a handful of sockets are not a power plan. Know where the circuit breakers are, available capacity and whether circuits are shared with the bar or kitchen. Otherwise, voltage may drop during the programme or lighting may go out when equipment at the bar is switched on.

A power plan identifies supply points, provides sufficient suitable cabling, keeps cables safely out of walkways or secured and assigns someone who can respond to a tripped breaker. These details separate a smooth event from chaos.
Mistake 4: lighting that is too bright, misdirected or completely wrong

Poor lighting damages the atmosphere and photo/video results. Excessively bright white light or spotlights aimed at faces make speakers look tired and guests uncomfortable. Too little lighting may feel stylish, but cameras cannot compensate for everything.

A practical minimum is a key light for the stage or speakers, ambient lighting that fills the space and a camera test on a phone. Check the actual image: if it looks poor on a phone, later footage will suffer too. Avoid shadows across faces and overly bright backgrounds.
Mistake 5: no plan for music and volume

Music is not simply about playing something. It should follow the event journey: arrivals, speeches, networking, peak moments and closing. Music that is too loud during networking shortens conversations. Music that is too quiet during an energetic section makes the room feel flat.
Agree on sound levels for each phase: entrance, speeches, breaks and networking. Give one person final authority; everyone having their own preference is a recipe for disorder.
The best technical production is the kind guests do not notice. They notice it only when something is wrong.
Quick checklist before guests arrive

Scheduled soundcheck and responsible person. Spare microphone and batteries. Power plan, cables and securing tape. Lighting tested on a phone. Music levels by event phase. One person who confirms the system is ready.
FAQ
What is the minimum technical setup for a small event?
A reliable microphone, clear sound and basic ambient lighting. Without these, everything else feels amateurish.
How do I prevent microphone feedback?
Position the speakers properly, configure EQ correctly and run a soundcheck. It is about setup, not luck.
